3. The instant petitioner as defendant husband contested the Family Suit pursuant to filing a written statement denying all the materials allegation stated in the plaint. The trial court on 21-1-2013 passed an exparte judgment and decree dated 21-1-2013 inter alga holding that the Opposite party wife is entitled to get Taka 40.000 as dower and maintenance and her one daughter is entitled to get Taka 3,000 + 3.000 = 6.000 only per month from on 1-1-2010 to 20-1-2013 as arrears and in future it will be continued as per law accordingly. 

 4. Thereafter the plaintiff decree holder filed Family Execution Case No. 01 of 2013 which was disposed of by the Execution Court when the defendant petitioner served out a civil imprisonent for a term of 3 (three) months and thereafter the opposite party as decree holder fi led another Family Execution Case being No. 02 of 2014 which is under adjudication and thereafter she filed two more Family Execution Cases Nos. 08 of 2014 and 01 of 2016. During pendency of Family Execution Cases No. 02 of 2014, subsequently the latter two cases were stayed on the ground that the Family Execution Suit No. 02 of 2014 is under adjudication. 

 5. The petitioner on 7-4-2015 paid Taka 50,000 by way of Chalan Receipt to the decree holder in the Family Execution Case No. 08 of 2014 and on 7-5-2014 paid Taka 5,000 and on 13-7-2015 paid Taka 5,000 in connection with the Family Execution Case No. 02 of 2014 which is now under adjudication. 

 7. Against the said order dated 5-5-2015 passed by the Family Execution Court, the decree holder opposite party preferred Family Miscellaneous Appeal No. 02 of 2015 before the learned Court of District Judge, Kushtia and the same was transferred to the learned Joint District Judge. 2nd Court. Kushtia for hearing. 

 12. Learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr. Al Amin submits that the Appellate Court unfairly and unjudiciously without considering the relevant provisions of law and without considering the background of the case vacated its own earlier order No. 15 dated 22-6-2016 thereby causing serious injustice to the petitioner. He submits that the application filed by the petitioner husband in Family Miscellaneous Appeal No. 02 of 2016 praying for producing evidence to prove the Talaknama dated 13-4-2012 and further praying to mark those as exhibits upon hearing the parties were made within the ambits of the Family Court Ordinance. 1985 and therefore the impugned order dated 28-9-2016 vacating the earlier order is an unlawful order and not sustainable. He submits that such application ought to have been allowed given that under the provisions of Family Courts Ordinance. 1985, the applicability of the provisions of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure is allowed since the provisions of section 16 of the Family Courts Ordinance 1985 specifically allows the application of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure including other provisions for the purpose of execution of a decree. He submits that it is evident from the records that the impugned order arises out of a pending appeal in execution of a decree under the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985. He continues that it is also obvious from the records that the Miscellaneous Appeal was filed by the opposite party wife for enforcement of the decree. He draws this court's attention to section 16 of the Ordinance of 1985. He reads section 16 (3) of the Ordinance which is reproduced here under: 

 "where the decree relates to the payment of money and the decretal amount is not paid within the time specified by the court, the decree shall, on the prayer of the decree holder to be made within a period of one year from the expiry of the time so specified, be executed— 

 (a) as a decree for money of a Civil Court under the Code, or 

 and on such execution the decretal amount recovered shall be paid to the decree holder." 

 13. Reverting to the facts of this case giving rise to the appeal he contends that it is obvious from the records that the plaintiff opposite party wife also filed the appeal by way of execution for payment of unpaid money. He argues that therefore the provisions of section l6(3)(a) and 3A are applicable in this case also. He next draws this court's attention to section 16(3A) of the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 wherefrom he points out that section 16(3A) of the Ordinance, 1985 expressly provides that "for the purpose of execution of decree under sub-section 3(a), the court shall be deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have all the powers of such Court under the Code" that is the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. He submits that Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 being enacted as a special law, Sub section 3A of section 16 of the Ordinance specifically provides that for purpose of execution of a decree the power of the court under the Code of Civil Procedure shall be applicable. Upon a query from this bench regarding the express bar in section 20 of the ordinance as to application and non application of certain laws in the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 except as otherwise expressly provided by or under the Ordinance, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that section 20 of the Ordinance expressly provides: "Save as otherwise expressly provided by or under this Ordinance, the provisions of the Evidence Act, 1872, and of the Code except sections 10 and 11 shall not apply to proceedings before the Family Courts." He points out that provisions of section 20 provides that no other sections except section 10 and 11 shall be applicable in the case under Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 in Family Suit whatsoever save or except as otherwise expressly provided by or under this Ordinance. He argues that in this case sub-section 3A of section 16 expressly and unambiguously provides that for the purpose of execution of a decree under sub-section (3)(a), the court meaning the Family Court shall be deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have all the powers of such Court under the Code. He argues that since sub-section 3A provides that for the purpose of execution of a decree the court shall be deemed to be a civil court therefore in the instant case Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure including the otherwise provisions of the Code for purpose of execution shall also be applicable. He submits that the appellate court upon total misapplication of mind vacated and revoked its own earlier order without properly interpreting the relevant provisions of law and without taking the facts of the case into consideration and therefore the order of the appellate court cannot be sustained and calls for interference. He concludes his submissions upon assertion that the judgments of the courts below ought to be set-aside and the Rule be made absolute for ends of justice. 

 14. On the other hand learned Advocate Mr. Shasti Sarker for the opposite party wife at the onset of his argument submits that the appellate court's order vacating its earlier order is correctly passed and does not call for interference in revision. He submits that section 20 of the Family Courts Ordinance expressly bars the application of the provisions of the Code except section 10 and 11 of the Code save as otherwise expressly provided by or under this ordinance. He assails that the petitioner prayed for producing some additional evidences which was initially incorrectly allowed upon misconception of facts and law but which was correctly revoked and vacated later by the same court. He submits that the provisions of section 16 of the Ordinance particularly sub-section 3 of section 16 only provides for a situation where an execution case is filed only for the purpose of execution and not for any other purpose. He contends that sub section 3A of section 16 also provides that for the purpose of execution of a decree only the provisions of the Code shall be applicable and not for any other purpose. He contends that therefore the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 being a Special law specially enacted and their being bar to the application of other laws under the Code except as those expressly provided for that is all the other provisions of the Code excepting those which are allowed shall not be applicable in a proceeding in a Family Court. In this context he cited a decision of this court in the case of Saleha Begum vs Dilruba Begum reported in 53 DLR (2(01) page-346 and submits that in this case also it was decided that the provisions of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure shall not he applicable due to the express bar in the law in section 20 of the Ordinance. He concludes his submissions upon assertion that therefore the impugned order does not call for interference and the Rule be discharged for ends of justice. 

 15. I have heard the learned Advocates from both sides perused the application and the materials on record including the judgments and orders of the courts below and read these alongside the relevant laws including the relevant provisions in the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985. From a perusal of the records it appears that the Family Miscellaneous Appeal No. 02 of 2015 was filed during the state of execution arising against the order of the Family Execution Court and appeal was filed by the opposite party wife. Therefore it is obvious that the impugned judgment and order and the background of such order also arises specifically out of an execution case which is primarily for the purpose of enforcement of a decree by way of payment of money by the husband to the wife. Upon further examination it also appears that the facts of this case also involves recovery of unpaid money. Therefore I find it imperative to examine the provisions of section 16 of the Ordinance of 1985 particularly the provisions of sub-section 3 and 3A of section 16 of the Ordinance. The provisions of section 16(3) and 3A are reproduced below:— 

 (3) "where the decree relates to the payment of money and the decretal amount is not paid within the time specified by the court, the decree shall on the prayer of the decree holder to be made within a period of one year from the expiry of the time so specified be executed— 

 (a) as a decree for money of a Civil Court under the Code, or 

 (b) as an order for payment of fine made by a Magistrate under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, and on such execution the decretal amount recovered shall be paid to the decree holder. 

 (3A) For the purpose of execution of a decree under sub-section (3)(a), the Court shall be deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have all the powers of such Court under the Code." 

 16. Upon perusal of section 16 (3)(a) and 3A of the Ordinance it is clear that this section contemplates a situation arising out of unpaid money followed by an execution case and further contemplates that where the amount is not paid the section also provides that the decree be executed as a decree for money in a Civil Court under the Code. 

 17. Next I feel it necessarily to draw my attention to sub section 3A of section 16 of the Ordinance which must be read together with sub-section 3(a). Upon scrutiny it is clear that sub-section 3A of section 16 expressly provides that for the purpose of execution of a decree under sub-section 3(a) the Family Court shall be deemed to be a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure and shall have all the powers of such court. 

 18. Upon perusal of the provisions of section 16(3)(a) and 3A it is my considered opinion that by providing that the family court while dealing with execution of a decree shall have all the powers of a civil court under the Code, the legislators intended that all the powers conferred upon a civil court that may be exercised by a civil court for purpose of execution of a decree including enforcement of decrees may also be conferred and exercised by a Family Court while enforcing a decree during the stage of execution thereof. 

 19. Learned Advocate for the opposite party argued that Section 20 provides a bar to the applicability of the Code in a Family Court proceeding save as those expressly provided for under the Ordinance. Upon perusal of the laws my considered understanding is that sub-section 3(a) and 3A of section 16 of the Ordinance of 1985 read together expressly provides and contemplate that a Family Court shall have all the powers of a civil court during the stage of execution while enforcing a decree. I do not find any ambiguity as such in the language of the said sub section 3A. By all the "powers" "under the Code" the legislators meant and intended that whatever powers have been vested in the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 for purpose of execution of a decree can also be exercised by a Family Court while enforcing a Decree through execution thereof. Such being the intention of the law, vesting a family court with all the powers of a civil court under the code, hence in this case the earlier order being Order No. 15 dated 22-6-2016 allowing the application directing the instant petitioner (husband) to produce documents by giving oral evidence under Order XLI, rule 27 of the code was correctly given. 

 22. “Save as" means "except" as otherwise expressly provided in the Ordinance. It is clear from the language that section 20 provides for exception in cases of "express" provision in the ordinance. As discussed elsewhere in this Judgment, sub-section 3A of section 16 `expressly' and clearly without any ambiguity provide that for purposes of enforcement of a decree under subsection 3(a) of Section 16, the Family Court shall be deemed to have "all the powers" of a Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 26. The facts arising out of the 53 DLR case involved a case for custody of a minor child and involved inter cilia the provisions of the Guardians and Wards Act (VIII of 1980). In the 53 DLR case this Division was not dealing with any issue arising out of execution of a decree in a Family Suit nor was it addressing the procedure of enforcement of any decree arising out of an execution case. In that case the provisions of section 16 sub-section 3(a) and /or sub-section 3A of section 16 of the ordinance or the horizon of its scope was not being dealt with or otherwise addressed at all. In that case the applicability of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure in an execution case arising out of a Family Suit under the provisions of section 16(3)(a) sub-section 3A was not the issue and the provisions of section 16 did not even feature anywhere in the horizon of that case. 

 29. After a minute thorough perusal of the provisions of Sub-section 3(a) and 3A of section 16 of the Ordinance, it is clear that however for purpose of execution the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 expressly provides that for purposes of execution of a decree the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 shall be applicable for enforcement of a decree in the absence of any ambiguity. I am inclined to hold that by enacting subsection 3A of section 16 the legislature expressly and specifically intended that for enforcement of a decree the powers of a civil court may be exercised by a Family Court and which also must include the provisions of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. Sub-section 3A of section 16 provides that the executing Court in a Family suit shall be vested with "all powers" of a court under the code. The language of the law providing for "all powers" under the code is plain and simple and easily understood.
